taxonomy.subtopic: Tissue transglutaminase, deamidated gliadin, and HLA-DQ2/DQ8

questions.stem_html:
A 30-year-old woman has chronic bloating, loose stools, iron deficiency, and an intensely pruritic vesicular eruption on the extensor surfaces of her elbows. Duodenal biopsy demonstrates villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Symptoms improve after eliminating wheat, barley, and rye.

Which molecular event is central to the intestinal immune response?

options.text_html: Pancreatic trypsin converts gliadin into a toxin that directly lyses enterocytes
Secretory IgA activates complement on villous epithelial cells
Tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin peptides, increasing their binding to HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8
Enterocytes lose CFTR function after gluten exposure
Bile acids covalently bind gliadin and induce granuloma formation

questions.explanation_html: Tissue transglutaminase modifies glutamine residues in gliadin, creating negatively charged peptides with enhanced affinity for HLA-DQ2/DQ8 on antigen-presenting cells. T-cell activation drives mucosal injury. Deamidated gliadin presentation through HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 links the dietary trigger to the adaptive immune response and characteristic villous damage.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Celiac disease is immune mediated and depends on antigen presentation, not direct enzymatic toxin formation.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: IgA antibodies are useful markers, but complement-mediated IgA cytotoxicity is not the central pathogenesis.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: CFTR dysfunction causes cystic fibrosis and is unrelated to gluten-triggered enteropathy.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Granulomas are not the characteristic lesion of celiac disease, and bile-acid conjugation is not the initiating event.

questions.educational_objective: Explain celiac disease through tissue-transglutaminase-mediated gliadin deamidation, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 presentation, and T-cell-mediated villous injury.
